questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before choosing any integration pattern, this course's framework says an architect needs answers to four questions: who initiates, how often, how much data, and how ________?
acceptedAnswers: fast does it need to be
questions.explain: The four framing questions are who initiates, how often, how much data, and how fast the response needs to be — the inputs that determine which integration pattern actually fits a requirement.

questions.prompt: A nightly order-sync integration fails to deliver 3,000 orders during a high-volume weekend, with no error logged anywhere. Which recurring integration failure category does this describe?
options: Silent data loss
Tight coupling to internal implementation details
No agreed-on error contract
API versioning failure
questions.explain: Silent data loss is a failure that produces no error and no alert, so records simply never arrive without anyone noticing — exactly the scenario described, where 3,000 orders vanished with nothing logged.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the number of point-to-point connections needed to fully connect N systems follows the formula N x (N-1) / ________.
questions.explain: The N-squared problem follows N x (N-1)/2 — with 6 systems, for example, that's 6x5/2 = 15 connections, illustrating how fast connections outgrow systems in a fully-meshed point-to-point design.

questions.prompt: In the hub-and-spoke model, what happens when a new system joins an integration landscape that already uses a middleware hub?
options: It needs a new connection to every existing system
It needs exactly one new connection — to the hub
It cannot join without rebuilding the hub from scratch
It needs N-1 new connections, where N is the number of existing systems
questions.explain: Hub-and-spoke turns connection growth linear: a new system connects once to the central hub rather than needing a direct connection to every other system, directly solving the N-squared problem.

questions.prompt: Match each component to the question it primarily answers.
right: Who is allowed to call this API, how often, and how do I protect the backend from being overwhelmed?
How does this message get translated and routed to the right backend, possibly across several steps?
questions.explain: An ESB answers the content-aware translation and routing question, while an API gateway answers the edge traffic-management and policy-enforcement question — related but distinct jobs.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of callouts a single Apex transaction can make, and what is the cumulative callout timeout cap across that transaction?
options: 10 callouts per transaction, with no cumulative cap at all
1,000 callouts per transaction, with a 10-second cumulative cap
100 callouts per transaction, with a 120-second cumulative timeout cap
50 callouts per transaction, with a 60-second cumulative cap
100 callouts per transaction, with no cumulative cap at all
There is no limit on callouts per transaction, only on individual callout timeout
questions.explain: Salesforce caps a single Apex transaction at 100 callouts, with cumulative callout time across the whole transaction capped at 120 seconds, additive across every callout made — per Salesforce's Apex Developer Guide.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E correctly states the 100-callout cap but wrongly claims there's no cumulative cap — Salesforce does enforce a 120-second cumulative cap across all callouts in a transaction, in addition to the per-transaction count limit, specifically to prevent one slow external system from indefinitely tying up shared compute resources.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about fire-and-forget vs. asynchronous request-reply.
options: Fire-and-forget is appropriate when the triggering system has no business reason to track the outcome of what it triggered
Asynchronous request-reply typically relies on a correlation identifier so a later reply can be matched back to the original request
Fire-and-forget requires tracking which outstanding requests are still waiting for a reply
Both sub-patterns remove the caller's blocking wait compared to synchronous communication
Asynchronous request-reply never needs any mechanism for the caller to learn the outcome
questions.explain: Fire-and-forget fits when the caller never needs to know the outcome, while request-reply tracks outstanding requests via a correlation ID so the caller can eventually learn the result. Both remove the caller's blocking wait, which is what makes them asynchronous in the first place.

questions.prompt: In event-driven architecture, what does "eventual consistency" mean, and for which kind of business process is it a genuine limitation rather than an acceptable trade-off?
options: Every consumer is guaranteed to process an event within exactly one second, with no exceptions
Eventual consistency means only one consumer out of many will ever receive the event
Eventual consistency is never an acceptable trade-off for any business process

All consumers will eventually reflect an event, but not necessarily at the same instant; it's a real limitation specifically for processes that need every system aligned on the same data at the same moment
questions.explain: Eventual consistency means every consumer eventually reflects an event's effect, but not simultaneously — fine for notifications and analytics, but a genuine limitation for a process that needs every system looking at exactly the same data right now.

questions.prompt: Match each API-led connectivity layer to its job.
right: Shaped exactly to a specific consumer's needs, often reusing a shared layer underneath
Sits closest to a backend system, exposing its data through a stable, implementation-hiding interface
Orchestrates business logic and combines data across one or more backend-facing APIs
questions.explain: System APIs sit closest to a backend and hide its implementation details. Process APIs orchestrate business logic across System APIs. Experience APIs shape the result for a specific consumer, often reusing one Process API across several different front ends.

questions.prompt: Match each named Enterprise Integration Pattern to what it does.
right: Converts a message from one format or structure to another
Decides where to send a message next, without altering its content
Collects multiple related messages and combines them into one consolidated message
Routes a message based on what's actually inside its content
questions.explain: A Message Router decides destination without altering content. A Message Translator converts format/structure. A Content-Based Router routes based on actual message content. An Aggregator collects related messages into one consolidated message.

questions.prompt: A requirement involves syncing 500,000 records nightly, with no one waiting on an immediate answer. What does this volume and urgency profile point toward, per this course's decision framework?
options: Bulk API or a scheduled batch pattern rather than synchronous, per-record calls
A synchronous, per-record REST API loop
A fire-and-forget Platform Event with no data payload
Point-to-point integration regardless of volume
questions.explain: High volume with tolerant timing rules out synchronous, per-record calls as impractical at scale and points toward a purpose-built large-volume mechanism like Bulk API or a scheduled batch pattern instead.

questions.prompt: What does request-reply messaging trade away, compared to RPC-style invocation, in exchange for resilience?
options: It trades away the ability to ever know the outcome of a remote operation
It trades away the simplicity of a call that feels like invoking a local function, decoupling the request and response through correlated messages instead
It trades away all data volume limits
It trades away the need for any correlation mechanism
questions.explain: RPC-style invocation is simple because it feels like a local function call, but it exposes the caller to the remote system's latency and failures directly. Request-reply messaging decouples the call using correlated messages, trading that simplicity for resilience.

questions.prompt: What is the main cost of a full sync approach compared to delta (incremental) sync?
options: Full sync cannot be scheduled on a fixed cadence
Full sync is incompatible with the Bulk API
Full sync re-sends every record on every run regardless of whether it changed, wasting processing capacity on a large dataset where only a small fraction changes daily
Full sync requires a correlation identifier for every record
questions.explain: Full sync's simplicity comes at a real cost: resending every record every run even when only a tiny fraction changed wastes both systems' processing capacity and runtime, a cost that grows directly with dataset size.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce implements data virtualization through Salesforce Connect, using ________ objects, whose data lives entirely in an external system rather than being stored in Salesforce.
questions.explain: Salesforce Connect's external objects behave like Salesforce objects in the UI and SOQL, but their data is never stored in Salesforce — each query reaches the external system live.

questions.prompt: What architectural problem do Named Credentials solve?
options: They eliminate the need for an API gateway entirely
They replace the need for any Apex code in an integration
They only work with the Bulk API, not with REST callouts
They bundle a callout's endpoint and authentication details into a single reusable reference, so credentials aren't hard-coded and can be rotated in one place
questions.explain: Named Credentials centralize where a callout's endpoint and authentication details live, so changing a Named Credential once updates every piece of code or Flow referencing it, instead of hunting down hard-coded secrets.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an integration operation to be idempotent?
options: Performing the operation multiple times produces the exact same result as performing it once
The operation can only ever be performed exactly one time, with no retries possible
The operation always completes within one second
The operation requires no network connection to complete
The operation can never fail under any circumstances
The operation automatically encrypts its payload before sending it
questions.explain: Idempotency is the property that running an operation multiple times produces the same result as running it once — making it safe to retry after an ambiguous failure, because even if the first attempt actually succeeded, retrying causes no harm.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B confuses idempotency with a one-time-only restriction. Idempotency is actually what MAKES repeated attempts safe — it doesn't forbid retries, it's the property that makes retries harmless even if the operation ends up running more than once.

questions.prompt: Why are exponential backoff and jitter normally used together in retry logic rather than either one alone?
options: Jitter alone removes the need for any maximum retry count
Backoff spaces out an individual caller's retries over increasing intervals, but callers that failed simultaneously would still retry in lockstep without jitter spreading that timing out
Backoff and jitter are two names for the exact same mechanism
Backoff only works for synchronous integrations and jitter only works for asynchronous ones
questions.explain: Backoff alone still lets many simultaneously-failed callers compute the same schedule and retry together at each step, re-creating a retry storm at a lower frequency; jitter adds randomized variation so those retries spread out instead of clustering.

questions.prompt: Match each integration governance pillar to the failure it exists to prevent.
right: Every team building and shipping integrations independently with no cross-check against the four-question framework
A routine change silently breaking an integration nobody remembers exists
An integration becoming an orphaned asset with no one positioned to fix it when it breaks
The fiftieth integration relearning decisions the first ten already settled
questions.explain: An inventory prevents forgotten integrations from breaking silently. Ownership prevents orphaned integrations with no one accountable. Standards prevent relearning the same decisions repeatedly. A review process prevents unchecked, independent shipping of new integrations.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
options: They are the same capability under two different names
Monitoring only applies to asynchronous integrations
Monitoring answers whether something is wrong right now; observability provides the deeper detail needed to understand why, once monitoring has flagged an issue
Observability replaces the need for any alerting
questions.explain: Monitoring watches defined signals and alerts on threshold breaches. Observability is the deeper capability — logged detail, tracing, context — needed to diagnose why an alerted issue is actually happening.

questions.prompt: Why does Salesforce enforce governor limits such as the Apex callout cap?
options: To generate additional licensing revenue regardless of actual usage
Because governor limits are an arbitrary legal requirement unrelated to platform architecture
To discourage customers from building any integrations at all
Because Salesforce is a multi-tenant platform, and without hard caps, one org's runaway process could degrade shared infrastructure performance for every other org
questions.explain: Governor limits exist because many organizations share the same underlying Salesforce infrastructure — a hard cap prevents one org's runaway process from monopolizing resources everyone else also depends on.

questions.prompt: Renaming a response field that existing callers depend on is an example of what kind of API change?
options: A breaking change, which justifies and requires a new API version
A backward-compatible change requiring no version bump
A deprecation policy
A rate-limiting change
questions.explain: Renaming a field breaks any existing caller depending on the original name — exactly the category of change that justifies a new API version rather than silently altering the version already in use.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a destination where a message goes after exhausting its retry attempts without succeeding, so a human or process can review it instead of it being silently dropped, is called a ________ queue.
questions.explain: A dead-letter queue is the deliberate alternative to both endless silent retries and silent data loss — it surfaces an exhausted failure for review.

questions.prompt: Select every item that belongs on this course's integration architecture review checklist.
options: Whether the proposed pattern actually matches the four-question analysis, or was chosen out of habit
Whether the core operation is idempotent or has an idempotency key if not naturally idempotent
Whether credentials are handled through a Named Credential rather than hard-coded
Whether the integration's developer personally prefers synchronous callouts
Whether the integration will be added to the org's integration inventory with a named owner
questions.explain: The review checklist covers pattern fit, failure semantics (idempotency, retry), security (Named Credentials), monitoring, and governance (inventory and ownership) — a developer's personal preference for a given pattern is explicitly not a valid justification.

questions.prompt: Why is comparing a vendor subscription's cost against zero a flawed way to evaluate build vs. buy for middleware?
options: Because subscription costs are always lower than build costs in every case
Because building in-house isn't free — it costs developer time to build and ongoing developer time to maintain, so a fair comparison uses total cost of ownership for both options
Because build decisions never require any ongoing maintenance
Because vendor subscriptions never have any ongoing cost after the first year
questions.explain: A fair build-vs-buy comparison accounts for the fully-loaded cost of building AND maintaining custom infrastructure over time (total cost of ownership), not a subscription's sticker price against an assumed-free in-house alternative.

questions.prompt: Match each element to what a complete integration landscape diagram should show for every connection.
right: Whether data flows one way or both ways between two systems
questions.explain: A complete diagram labels direction (one-way vs. bidirectional), pattern (synchronous, async, batch, event-driven), and frequency (real-time, nightly, hourly, on-demand) for every connection, alongside the systems themselves.

questions.prompt: In the order-management case study, why did Flow 3 (shipping-rate calculation at checkout) justify synchronous communication while Flow 1 (order creation sent to the WMS) used an asynchronous pattern?
options: Flow 3 involves more data volume than Flow 1
Flow 1 uses a different programming language than Flow 3
The rep in Flow 3 is blocked waiting and cannot proceed without an immediate answer, while the WMS in Flow 1 only needs the order within minutes, not milliseconds
Synchronous communication is always preferred whenever money is involved
questions.explain: The deciding factor is the urgency answer for each flow: Flow 3's rep genuinely cannot proceed without an immediate rate, justifying synchronous communication, while Flow 1's WMS tolerates a short delay, making an asynchronous pattern with an idempotency key the better fit.

questions.prompt: In the Customer 360 case study, why was product-usage telemetry virtualized via Salesforce Connect rather than replicated into Salesforce?
options: Because telemetry data cannot be accessed through any API
Because virtualized data is always more secure than replicated data
Because the finance system required it to be virtualized
Because it is enormous in volume, changes constantly, and is only occasionally viewed by a rep, making full replication wasteful
questions.explain: Telemetry's high volume, constant change rate, and infrequent viewing is exactly the profile that favors virtualization over replication — avoiding storing large amounts of data that's rarely actually queried.

questions.prompt: A scenario question states that three independent systems must react to a Contract being activated, and explicitly requires that adding a fourth system next year should not require changing the Contract-activation logic. Which pattern does this requirement point to almost by name?
options: Event-driven architecture, because of its explicit producer/consumer decoupling
Point-to-point integration
A one-time data migration
Synchronous RPC-style invocation
questions.explain: The explicit requirement that a new consumer shouldn't require changing the producer is exactly EDA's decoupling benefit — any point-to-point-style answer requiring the producer to change for a new consumer is wrong by definition here.

questions.prompt: What are reviewers in Salesforce's Certified Technical Architect (CTA) review board actually evaluating, per this course?
options: Whether the candidate proposed the one single "correct" architecture
Whether the candidate can justify their specific design choices with sound reasoning, identify the trade-offs accepted, and respond credibly to pushback — multiple reasonable designs can pass
Whether the candidate memorized the most governor limit numbers
Whether the candidate's design exactly matches a fixed answer key
questions.explain: The CTA review board doesn't require one specific 'correct' design — what's evaluated is the quality of the candidate's reasoning, trade-off awareness, and ability to defend choices credibly under direct questioning.

questions.prompt: Put these elements of a strong defense of a design decision, as taught in this course's review-board practice lesson, in the order they should be presented.
items: State the decision that was made
State the specific facts from the scenario that drove it
State the trade-off being accepted and why it's acceptable given those facts
Name at least one alternative that was considered and explain why it was rejected
questions.explain: A strong defense follows this order: name the decision, ground it in the specific facts that drove it, state the trade-off being accepted and its justification, and name a rejected alternative with reasoning — giving a reviewer a complete, well-reasoned case rather than a bare assertion.
